title: Year three close: the great story
hook: the whole story from the palace to today

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole year in one sitting: the Buddhacarita's poem and all that followed it. Your line: look how far.

A gate opens at night, and a prince rides out of his father's palace. In the poem that opened this year, that night is the turning point of the great story. It doesn't end there, and it doesn't end with him. It runs on, hand to hand, road to road, to a temple down some street near you, a lamp on a windowsill, a person sitting still for two minutes on an ordinary morning. Today, the last day of year three: the whole story, from that gate to today.
screen: `A GATE OPENS AT NIGHT.` → `HAND TO HAND, ROAD TO ROAD.` → `FROM THE GATE TO TODAY.`

segments.voice: The prince sees age, sickness and death, and a wanderer at peace, and he leaves. He strives until he is thin as a shadow. He sits beneath a tree; Mara comes with his army of desire and doubt, and the seeker doesn't get up. He wakes up. At the deer park he turns the wheel of the teaching for his old companions. Friends come, then strangers, then kings and courtesans and outcasts. Women ask to be ordained, and an order of nuns begins. For years he walks the roads and teaches, and at the end, lying between two trees, he gives his last instruction, the one you heard on the day of renewal: in paraphrase, all made things come apart, so keep going with care. Then the story passes to other hands. The elders meet and recite what they remember. Reciters carry it by memory; later, tradition says, scribes write it down. An emperor carves teachings into stone. Monks and nuns carry it south across the sea and north along the caravan roads, into new languages. Teachers argue, explain, and build new schools on it. Buddhists tell some parts differently: which texts come first, which teachers matter most. Each school keeps its own telling. Then the hard chapters: monasteries burned, monks killed, texts lost. And each time, someone gathers what's left and begins again. Which brings the story here: to temples far from where it started, to chaplains in hospitals, to festivals with sweet tea and lamps. A story that started with one person leaving home is now kept by people in many homes.
screen: `THE PALACE, THE TREE, THE DEER PARK.` · `KEEP GOING WITH CARE.` · `MEMORY, STONE, ROADS AND SCHOOLS.` · then, large: `BROKEN, AND BEGUN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: If there's a window near you, turn toward it; if not, a doorway, or the far side of the room. Let your eyes rest there without naming anything, and let your attention go out the way the story went through the palace gate, gently, then back to the breath. Nothing to finish; just rest.
Buddha. The awakened one at the center of the great story, from the palace gate to the people keeping it today, and the end of the third year on this path. Today's word.
Your line: you know the story now. Tomorrow, year four opens with the higher teaching. Year three, complete.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Buddha's life and the story of the teaching at festivals, in temple paintings and in chanting, and some communities close a year of study by dedicating its merit to others.

fork.setup: you've heard the whole story, from the palace gate to today. the year is over. what does the path ask of you now?
fork.reveal: the last day of the year asks only for rest and a long look out, the way the story itself went out through the gate.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the title of the one at the center of the story, usually given in English as the awakened one.

trapdoor: what you thought: the life story of one man.
what it means: a story that runs from a palace gate to a temple down your road, carried by many hands.
what a scholar hears: one story kept in many kinds of text, poem, sutta, monastic rule, commentary and chronicle, with each school keeping its own telling.
recall: one on the way to awakening, for others
a flame going out; the path's goal

chat.says: Did the Buddha's story end when he died?
options: No: it passed hand to hand, road to road, all the way to today.
Yes: after he died, the teaching stayed with his family only.
No: he wrote it all down himself before he passed away.
chat.meaning: After his death, the elders recited it, reciters carried it, and monks and nuns took it across the sea and the caravan roads to today.

Buddha.meaning: the awakened one, at the center of the great story

Mara.meaning: the tempter, with his army of desire and doubt

deer park.meaning: where the Buddha first taught his old companions

notes: Last words quoted from T. W. Rhys Davids' translation of the Mahaparinibbana Suttanta (SBE XI, 1881 / Dialogues II, 1910): verify exact wording and punctuation.
'Five old companions' at the deer park: the script says only 'his old companions' (the group of five), leaving the number out under the claims rule.
'Lying between two trees' (the twin sala trees at Kusinara) is in DN 16; confirm.
Emperor carving teachings into stone refers to Ashoka's edicts; monks and nuns carried south (Mahinda and Sanghamitta per the Mahavamsa); left unnamed and undated deliberately.
The howItsDone line says 'some communities' dedicate merit at the close of study; soften if a Keeper prefers.
Year-three close: tomorrow opens year four (Abhidhamma).

Editor pass: the hook said the Buddhacarita 'begins' the story at the night departure, but the poem opens with the birth; now called the turning point. The last-words quotation repeated day 1051's centerpiece ten days earlier, so it is paraphrased and pointed back to that day, the screen line and a myth item were replaced, and the source set to paraphrase. 'Then scribes write it down' softened to 'later, tradition says'.

Audit pass: garbled pointer to day 1051 ('the one heard on this path when it spoke of renewal') rewritten; 'they keep their tellings side by side' (an unsourced claim about how schools coexist) changed to 'each school keeps its own telling'.
